title: Shakira and Burna Boy’s ‘Dai Dai’ Aims to Be the Next ‘Waka Waka’—and Raise $100 Million
summary:
Sixteen years after “Waka Waka” became the unofficial soundtrack of the 2010 World Cup, Shakira is back with a new contender: “Dai Dai,” a collaboration with Nigerian superstar Burna Boy. Released Friday, the track is a vibrant fusion of Latin pop and Afrobeats, laced with multilingual chants—“come on” in Italian, English, Japanese, French, and Spanish—and a roll call of soccer icons from Pelé to Cristiano Ronaldo.

But this isn’t just a party anthem. FIFA says all royalties will support its Global Citizen Education Fund, aiming to raise $100 million for children’s education and soccer programs by the tournament’s end on July 19. “It captures the energy, passion and global spirit that will define the greatest show on earth,” FIFA declared.

Shakira is no stranger to World Cup stages. Her 2010 hit with South Africa’s Freshlyground earned a Guinness World Record for most-streamed FIFA song on Spotify (over a billion plays). She also performed “Hips Don’t Lie” at the 2006 closing ceremony and “La La La” in 2014. “She’s good at incorporating gestures towards other cultures,” says Brent Keogh, a music lecturer at the University of Technology Sydney. “She can pull on these things and bring it into this global pop package.”

Burna Boy, dubbed the “African Giant,” brings his own heavyweight credentials: the first solo Nigerian Grammy winner and first African artist to sell out a U.S. stadium. Together, they represent FIFA’s strategic push to appeal to Latin and sub-Saharan African audiences, says ethnomusicologist Eduardo Herrera. “This is purposefully FIFA’s effort to have a successful song by bringing in artists that they know are going to appeal to at least two large numbers of the population.”

The song arrives as FIFA amps up the spectacle: Shakira, Madonna, and BTS will headline the inaugural halftime show at the final in New Jersey. It’s a far cry from the 1930s, when local musicians provided the soundtrack. The modern era of official anthems took off with Ricky Martin’s “La Copa de la Vida” in 1998, which ignited the “Latin Explosion” and proved a World Cup song could launch global careers. “Dai Dai” aims to do the same, blending sport, charity, and a beat you can’t ignore.
why_it_matters: The World Cup’s marriage of music, charity, and marketing shows how global organisations shape culture and who benefits—a lesson in how entertainment can drive social change and corporate branding that affects your media choices.

background_read: The FIFA World Cup has had official songs since at least 1962, but the modern era of pop anthems began with Ricky Martin’s “La Copa de la Vida” for the 1998 tournament, which sparked the so-called “Latin Explosion” in global music.
Shakira later made history with “Waka Waka” in 2010, recorded with South African group Freshlyground; it remains the most-streamed FIFA song on Spotify.
Burna Boy (born Damini Ogulu) is a central figure in Afrobeats, a genre blending West African rhythms with pop and dancehall, and his rise reflects Africa’s growing influence on worldwide charts.

FIFA (the Fédération Internationale de Football Association) is the global governing body for football, organizing the World Cup every four years, and it often uses music to promote its message of unity.
The new halftime show at the final in New Jersey, featuring artists like Madonna and BTS alongside Shakira, signals a shift toward Super Bowl-style entertainment.

perspectives.description: FIFA showcases the song’s royalties going to education as a win-win—entertainment that funds real-world projects, potentially improving the lives of disadvantaged children.
Critics might see the charity angle as a distraction from FIFA’s own controversies, such as worker conditions in host nations, using music to polish its image while avoiding deeper accountability.
Experts note that combining a Latin icon with an Afrobeats star is a strategic move to dominate global streaming charts, showing how the World Cup is now a marketing platform for labels and artists.

The halftime show signals that football is adopting American-style entertainment, which could change how young fans experience the sport—making music and celebrity as central as the game itself, potentially altering sports culture for your generation.
